pedagogy.summary: This topic is fluency with C = πd (= 2πr) and A = πr², and applying them to composite shapes with circular parts. Best taught by deriving both from the meaning of π rather than memorising two similar-looking formulae: π is the constant ratio of every circle's circumference to its diameter (a little over 3), so C = πd is almost a definition; and A = πr² comes from cutting the circle into thin wedges and rearranging them into a near-rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r. The two persistent hazards are confusing radius with diameter, and swapping the circumference and area formulae — both eased by keeping the meaning of each in view (circumference is a length, area is a covering in square units).
bestPractices: Establish π as circumference ÷ diameter — measure round several circular objects and divide by the diameter to find it is always ≈ 3.14; this makes C = πd meaningful, not arbitrary
Derive A = πr² by cutting the circle into wedges and rearranging into a near-rectangle of length πr and height r (πr × r = πr²)
Drill the radius/diameter link (d = 2r) explicitly and check which the formula needs before substituting — circumference uses d (or 2r), area uses r²
Distinguish 'squaring' from 'doubling': r² means r × r, not 2r; area grows with the square of the radius, giving square units
For composite shapes, decompose into a rectangle plus a semicircle, find each part, then add — watching which lengths are the circle's radius
Keep dimensions and units in view: circumference is a length (cm), area is a covering (cm²)
keyRepresentations: A circle with radius, diameter and circumference labelled; the d = 2r link
π as the ratio of circumference to diameter (a string round a tin measured against the diameter, ≈ 3.14)
The circle cut into wedges rearranged into a near-rectangle of length πr and height r (derivation of πr²)
A composite shape decomposed into a rectangle plus a semicircle
Unit labels distinguishing length (cm) from area (cm²)
commonMisconceptions: Confusing radius and diameter — substituting the diameter where the radius is needed (or vice versa)
Swapping the circumference and area formulae (using πr² for circumference or 2πr for area)
Forgetting to square the radius, or squaring as 'doubling' (treating r² as 2r or as the diameter)
Giving an area in linear units, or a circumference in square units
On composite shapes, using the diameter as the radius of the semicircle, or dropping a straight edge from the perimeter

learn.summary: Pupils (ages ~12–14) build fluency with C = πd (= 2πr) and A = πr² and apply them to composite shapes with circular parts. The emphasis is on deriving both formulae from the meaning of π — the constant ratio of every circle's circumference to its diameter, a little over 3 — rather than memorising two similar-looking formulae. π is almost a definition of C = πd; A = πr² follows from cutting a circle into thin wedges and rearranging them into a near-rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r. The two persistent hazards are confusing radius with diameter, and swapping the circumference and area formulae; both are eased by keeping each quantity's meaning and units in view (circumference is a length in cm, area is a covering in cm²).

activities.title: Discover π by unrolling the circumference
feedback: If your ratios differ wildly between circles, re-check your measurements — the string should wrap exactly once with no slack, and the diameter must pass through the centre and be measured where the string wraps; all circles should give roughly the same value close to 3.14, with small differences due to measurement error.
Prompt: 'Roughly how many diameters fit around the edge of a circle, and what do we call that number?'

If a learner thinks π changes with circle size, point to their own table of results showing roughly the same value (close to 3.14) for every circle, and explain that the small differences come from measurement error, not from π changing.
activities.rationale: Grounding π as a measured ratio addresses the vague-notion-of-π misconception and makes C = πd meaningful rather than memorised. An optional interactive 'roll the circle' animation — laying the circumference along a line marked in diameters — can make the ≈ 3.14 result vivid, but physical measurement of real objects achieves the same discovery.
sourceClaims: Learners confuse 'squaring' the radius with 'doubling' it (treating r² as equivalent to the diameter), reason about area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and hold vague notions of π rather than seeing it as the ratio of circumference to diameter
learnerActions: Take several circular objects (tins, lids, cups) of different sizes; wrap a string once around each and measure that length, then measure the diameter across each.

Divide each circumference by its diameter and record the result; notice the results are all close to the same value, a little over 3 (near π ≈ 3.14, allowing for small measurement errors), whatever the size of the circle.
Lay the measured circumference along a line marked off in lengths equal to that circle's own diameter, and see that it reaches to just past three diameters.
State in your own words: C = πd means the way round is 'a bit more than 3 diameters'.
activities.intendedInsight: π is the fixed ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter (≈ 3.14), so C = πd is almost a definition, not an arbitrary formula to recall.

activities.title: Build the area formula by rearranging wedges
feedback: If a learner labels the length as the full circumference, remind them each long edge of the rearranged shape is made of only half the arcs, so the length is πr, not 2πr.
Prompt: 'Which of your two results is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?'
If the height is mislabelled as the diameter, point back to the wedge: its straight side is the radius.
activities.rationale: Deriving πr² from decomposition addresses treating area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and helps keep area distinct from circumference. An optional drag-the-wedges tool that builds the πr × r rectangle can reinforce the same idea; paper cutting achieves it concretely. Note that a paper circle has slight thickness and models the ideal zero-thickness plane figure it represents — reason about the mathematical circle, not the card.
sourceClaims: Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r

Learners confuse 'squaring' the radius with 'doubling' it (treating r² as equivalent to the diameter), reason about area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and hold vague notions of π rather than seeing it as the ratio of circumference to diameter
learnerActions: Cut a paper circle into a number of thin equal wedges (sectors) and fan them out, alternating points up and down, to form a shape close to a rectangle (parallelogram).
Identify the height of the near-rectangle as the radius r, and its length as half the way round the circle — half the circumference, which is πr.
Compute the area of the near-rectangle as length × height = πr × r = πr², and connect this to the circle's area.
Explain why cutting into more, thinner wedges makes the shape look more like a true rectangle.
activities.intendedInsight: A = πr² is a product of a length (πr) and a length (r) giving square units, derived from rearranging the circle — not a lookalike string to confuse with C = πd.

activities.title: Radius-or-diameter: check before you substitute
feedback: If a learner computes π × 10² = 100π for area in the diameter-given case, flag that they used the diameter as the radius — halve it first: r = 5, A = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm².
If a learner reports area as π × 2 × 5 or π × 10, they have doubled instead of squared — r² means r × r, the area of a little square of side r.
Prompt: 'You were given the diameter — why can't you put it straight into πr²?'
Prompt: 'If the radius doubled, what happens to the circumference, and what happens to the area?' (area ×4, not ×2).
activities.rationale: Making the radius/diameter check an explicit first step and distinguishing squaring from doubling target the two most flagged hazards. An optional radius/diameter toggle that recomputes C and A, and flags a squared-vs-doubled slip, can make the check vivid; the self-check questions work on paper too.
sourceClaims: Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r

Learners confuse 'squaring' the radius with 'doubling' it (treating r² as equivalent to the diameter), reason about area as a sum of lengths rather than a product in square units, and hold vague notions of π rather than seeing it as the ratio of circumference to diameter
learnerActions: For each problem, first write 'What am I given — radius or diameter?' and 'What does this formula need?' before substituting.
Given a diameter of 10 cm, find the area: halve it to get r = 5 cm, then compute A = π × 5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² (not π × 10²).
Given a radius of 5 cm, find both the circumference C = π × 10 = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm and the area A = π × 5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm².
Investigate: if the radius doubles, what happens to the circumference and to the area? Confirm circumference doubles (×2) but area quadruples (×4).
activities.intendedInsight: Circumference uses d (or 2r) and area uses r²; you must convert a given diameter to a radius before using πr², and squaring is r × r (not doubling), so area grows with the square of the radius.

activities.title: Composite shapes: rectangle plus semicircle
feedback: If a learner uses r = 4 for the semicircle, remind them 4 cm is the diameter across the short end; the radius is 2 cm.
If a learner leaves in a straight edge where the semicircle joins (or omits the arc), re-trace the boundary: the arc takes the place of that edge.
Prompt: 'Which of your answers is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?'
Check: did you keep straight which number is the radius for each circular part?
activities.rationale: Decomposing and tracing the real boundary addresses using the diameter as the semicircle's radius and dropping/adding wrong edges in the perimeter. An optional composite-shape builder that shows each part's contribution can scaffold this; careful labelled sketching achieves the same decomposition.
sourceClaims: Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r
Pupils commonly confuse area and perimeter, which for circles surfaces as swapping circumference (a length) with area (square units)
KS3 pupils should calculate the circumference and area of circles and solve problems involving the perimeters and areas of composite shapes that include circular parts
learnerActions: Take a composite shape — e.g. a rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm with a semicircle of diameter 4 cm on one short (4 cm) end — and sketch it, labelling every given length.
Find the semicircle's radius as half its diameter (here r = 2 cm), not the full width.
For the area, add the rectangle's area to half the circle's area: 10 × 4 + ½ × π × 2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm².
For the perimeter, trace the actual boundary: include the rectangle's exposed edges plus the semicircle arc (½ × π × diameter = ½ × π × 4 = 2π), with NO straight edge where the semicircle sits.
State the units: area in cm², perimeter in cm.
activities.intendedInsight: Composite shapes are decomposed into parts whose areas are added, while the perimeter follows the true outline — the arc replaces the covered straight edge, and the semicircle's radius is half its diameter.

activities.title: Formula-choice and unit checks (retrieval practice)
feedback: If the two answers are switched (circumference in cm², area in cm), you have swapped the formulae — anchor each to what it measures: circumference from πd is a length, area from πr² is a covering.
If a method is correct but the unit is wrong, re-check the unit against what was calculated — don't re-derive, just correct the label.
If a diameter distractor is chosen in πr², note the full width was used instead of the radius — halve the diameter to the radius first.
activities.rationale: Spaced retrieval with targeted distractors (diameter-in-πr², swapped formulae, wrong units) consolidates fluency and surfaces residual misconceptions, including the radius/diameter slip. Scored recognition and matching tasks assess and rehearse choices but do not by themselves require independent derivation or transfer to a novel composite figure — pair with the construction activities above.
sourceClaims: Pupils commonly confuse area and perimeter, which for circles surfaces as swapping circumference (a length) with area (square units)

Pupils must know d = 2r and be able to convert between radius and diameter; confusion among the variables C, d and r is a flagged hazard; A = πr² is derived by decomposing the circle into wedges rearranged into a rectangle of length πr (half the circumference) and height r
learnerActions: Match each circle to its correct circumference and area expressions, watching for distractors that use πr² for circumference or 2πr for area.
Answer a question whose tempting wrong choice uses the diameter in πr² — reject it by halving to the radius first.
For each completed calculation, label the result with its unit and justify: a distance round is cm, a covering is cm².
Given a diameter, first find the radius before applying πr².
activities.intendedInsight: Keeping the two formulae distinct and attaching correct units (cm for circumference, cm² for area) consolidates the derived understanding, while converting a given diameter to a radius before using πr² guards the most common slip.

constraints: Learners should be able to convert between radius and diameter (d = 2r) and to find the area of a rectangle before this topic; semicircle composite work also builds on perimeter/area of composite shapes.

Recognition and matching tasks (matching circles to formulae, multiple-choice with distractors) are useful for rehearsal and assessment but do not require independent derivation or application to a novel figure; they should supplement, not replace, the measurement, wedge-rearranging, and composite-construction activities.

A static labelled circle with tap-to-reveal can name radius, diameter and circumference and display both formulae, but cannot let a learner derive π, rearrange the wedges, or apply the formulae to a new shape — treat it as a reference scaffold, not the main learning activity.

Paper circles and string-and-tin measurements are physical approximations of ideal plane figures (paper and card have slight thickness); use them to approximate the mathematical circle and reason about the represented figure rather than the physical cutout.

Interactive features named here (roll-the-circle animation, drag-the-wedges tool, radius/diameter toggle, composite-shape builder, unit labels) are optional ways to make the mechanism concrete — they are illustrative, not mandatory; the same insights are reachable with physical materials and sketching.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of a saved teaching-research row without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. The activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions, and cited claims support teaching principles/misconceptions rather than proving any specific activity was tested or superior to another medium.

Worked values were independently checked: for a diameter of 10 cm, r = 5 cm, A = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² and C = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm; using the diameter wrongly gives π × 10² = 100π ≈ 314 cm². For the composite shape (10×4 rectangle, semicircle of diameter 4 ⇒ r = 2): area = 40 + ½π·2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm²; the semicircle arc = ½·π·4 = 2π. These match the source's correctAnswer.

The KS3 national-curriculum source is marked verified:false in the row; it is cited only for the composite-shape objective in the composite activity, with the verified NCTM claim supporting the radius-is-half-diameter decomposition principle. No efficacy is claimed for it, and it is a topical/curriculum requirement rather than a teaching-principle claim.

The original source claimed a 3D artefact 'adds nothing' and that unscripted dialogue does not serve this skill; these were catalog fit judgements and have been softened — circle circumference and area are planar, so 3D is not required here, and calculation practice benefits from doing-and-checking, but no universal claim of necessity or exclusion is asserted.

The source stated a static tap-to-reveal image 'cannot' let the child derive or apply; retained only as a narrowly scoped affordance limitation (it is a reference scaffold), not as a universal law about static images.

probeDeeper: 'You were given the diameter — why can't you put it straight into πr²?' — forcing the radius/diameter distinction
'Which of your answers is a length and which is an area? How can you tell from the units?' — separating circumference from area
'If the radius doubled, what happens to the circumference, and what happens to the area?' — a counterexample exposing square-vs-linear growth (area ×4, not ×2)
'Roughly how many diameters fit around the edge of a circle, and what do we call that number?' — probing π as a ratio
assess.correctAnswer: (a) C = π×10 = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm; A = π×5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm². (b) radius = 5 cm, so A = π×5² = 25π ≈ 78.5 cm² (NOT π×10²). (c) perimeter = the rectangle's exposed edges plus the semicircle arc (½×π×4 = 2π), with no straight edge where the semicircle sits; area = 10×4 + ½×π×2² = 40 + 2π ≈ 46.3 cm². π is the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter, a little over 3. Circumference in cm, area in cm².

errorPatterns.pattern: Confuses radius and diameter — substitutes the diameter where the radius is needed ('the size across is 10, so r² is 10²')
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reteach d = 2r and make 'which do I have, which does the formula need?' an explicit first step; halve a diameter to the radius before substituting
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (b) computes π×10² = 100π instead of π×5²; uses the full width in πr²

errorPatterns.pattern: Swaps the circumference and area formulae — uses πr² for circumference or 2πr (or πd) for area
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor each formula to what it measures — circumference is the distance round (a length, from πd), area is the covering (square units, from πr²); derive both so they are not two lookalike strings
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Reports the circumference in square units or the area as a linear multiple of the radius; the two answers are switched

errorPatterns.pattern: Forgets to square the radius, or 'squares' by doubling — treats r² as 2r or as the diameter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Make squaring explicit as r × r (the area of a little square), distinct from doubling; show the area is a covering that grows with r², not the diameter
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (a)/(b) computes π×2×5 or π×10 for the area instead of π×5²; equates r² with the diameter

errorPatterns.pattern: On the composite shape, uses the semicircle's DIAMETER as its radius, or includes/omits the wrong edges in the perimeter
errorPatterns.nextMove: Decompose explicitly: label each part, identify the semicircle's radius (half its diameter), and trace the actual boundary for the perimeter, arc replacing the covered edge
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On (c) uses r = 4 for the semicircle, or adds a straight edge where the arc replaces it (or omits the arc)

errorPatterns.pattern: Gives area in linear units or circumference in square units
errorPatterns.nextMove: Prompt 'a distance round is cm, a covering is cm²'; check the unit against what was calculated rather than reteaching
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Method correct but the unit is wrong — cm for an area or cm² for a circumference

responseLevels.gap: Cannot calculate reliably — uses the diameter in πr², swaps circumference and area, or doubles instead of squaring; units muddled
responseLevels.full: Calculates circumference and area correctly, converting diameter to radius as needed, keeps the two formulae distinct and can explain π as a ratio and A = πr² informally, handles composite shapes with circular parts, and uses correct linear/square units — transferring to a novel composite figure
responseLevels.partial: Uses the formulae correctly when handed the radius directly, but is caught by a diameter-given problem, cannot say why the formulae work or what π is, or mishandles the semicircle in a composite shape — has two formulae as strings, not a derived, distinguished pair

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give the child a calculator and three tasks: (a) a circle with radius 5 cm — find its circumference and its area; (b) a circle given by its DIAMETER of 10 cm — find its area; (c) a composite shape: a rectangle 10 cm by 4 cm with a semicircle of diameter 4 cm on one short end — find the perimeter and the area. Also ask them to explain, roughly, what π has to do with a circle. Watch whether they use the radius (not the diameter) in πr², whether they keep circumference and area formulae apart, whether they square rather than double the radius, and whether they use square units for area.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands halves the diameter to a radius before using πr² and keeps the two formulae distinct; a child with the classic error uses the diameter in the area formula (π×10² = 314) or squares πr rather than r, giving a wildly different answer traceable to one mistake. The diameter-given circle (b) directly separates those who track radius vs diameter, and asking about π distinguishes derived understanding from formula-recall.
